L416: # Compiler and flags
L417: NVCC := nvcc
L418: NVCC_FLAGS := -O3 -arch=native -std=c++17
L419: INCLUDE_FLAGS := -Iinclude -Iicicle
L420: # Target executable
L421: TARGET := sumcheck.bin
L422: 
L423: # Source file
L424: SRC := src/sumcheck_cuda.cu
L425: 
L426: # Default field to use
L427: USE_FIELD ?= useM31ext3
L428: 
L429: # Set the minimum required version
L430: NVCC_MIN_VERSION := 12.5
L431: 
L432: # Get NVCC version
L433: NVCC_VERSION := $(shell $(NVCC) --version | grep -oP 'release \K[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' | head -n 1)
L434: NVCC_MAJOR := $(shell echo $(NVCC_VERSION) | cut -d. -f1)
L435: NVCC_MINOR := $(shell echo $(NVCC_VERSION) | cut -d. -f2)
L436: 
L437: # Phony targets
L438: .PHONY: all check_nvcc clean
L439: # Default target
L440: all: check_nvcc $(TARGET)
L441: 
L442: # Check NVCC version
L443: check_nvcc:
L444: @if ! command -v $(NVCC) > /dev/null 2>&1; then \
L445: echo "Error: $(NVCC) is not installed."; \
L446: exit 1; \
L447: elif [ $(NVCC_MAJOR) -lt 12 ] || ([ $(NVCC_MAJOR) -eq 12 ] && [ $(NVCC_MINOR) -lt 5 ]); then \
L448: echo "Error: $(NVCC) version must be >= $(NVCC_MIN_VERSION). Current version: $(NVCC_VERSION)"; \
L449: exit 1; \
L450: else \
L451: echo "$(NVCC) version $(NVCC_VERSION) is sufficient."; \
L452: fi

L13@P1: Abstract. The sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMxV) is a kernel operation widely used in iterative linear
L14@P1: solvers. The same sparse matrix is multiplied by a dense vector repeatedly in these solvers. Matrices with irregular
L15@P1: sparsity patterns make it difficult to utilize cache locality effectively in SpMxV computations. In this work, we
L16@P1: investigate single- and multiple-SpMxV frameworks for exploiting cache locality in SpMxV computations. For the
L17@P1: single-SpMxV framework, we propose two cache-size-aware top-down row/column-reordering methods based on 1D

For an effective matrix splitting required in this framework, we propose a cachesize-aware top-down approach based on 2D sparse matrix partitioning by utilizing the row-column-net hypergraph
L21@P1: model. For this framework, we also propose two methods for effective ordering of individual SpMxV operations.
L22@P1: The primary objective in all of the three methods is to maximize the exploitation of temporal locality. We evaluate
L23@P1: the validity of our models and methods on a wide range of sparse matrices using both cache-miss simulations and
L24@P1: actual runs by using OSKI. Experimental results show that proposed methods and models outperform state-of-the-art
L25@P1: schemes.
L26@P1: Key words. cache locality, sparse matrix, matrix-vector multiplication, matrix reordering, computational hypergraph model, hypergraph partitioning, traveling salesman problem

L28@P1: 1. Introduction. Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMxV) is an important kernel
L29@P1: operation in iterative linear solvers used for the solution of large, sparse, linear systems of
L30@P1: equations. In these iterative solvers, the SpMxV operation y ←Ax is repeatedly performed
L31@P1: with the same large, irregularly sparse matrix A. Irregular access pattern during these repeated SpMxV operations causes poor usage of CPU caches in today’s deep memory hierarchy technology. However, SpMxV operation has a potential to exhibit very high performance
L32@P1: gains if temporal and spatial localities are respected and exploited properly. Here, temporal locality refers to the reuse of data words (e.g., x-vector entries) within relatively small
L33@P1: time durations, whereas spatial locality refers to the use of data words (e.g., matrix nonzeros)
L34@P1: within relatively close storage locations (e.g., in the same lines).
L35@P1: In this work, we investigate two distinct frameworks for the SpMxV operation: singleSpMxV and multiple-SpMxV frameworks. In the single-SpMxV framework, the y -vector
L36@P1: results are computed by performing a single SpMxV operation y ← Ax. In the multipleSpMxV framework, y ← Ax operation is computed as a sequence of multiple input- and
L37@P1: output-dependent SpMxV operations, y ← y + Akx for k = 1, . . . , k , where A = A1 +

L39@P1: reordering methods based on top-down 1D and 2D partitioning of a given sparse matrix. The
L40@P1: 1D-partitioning-based method relies on transforming a sparse matrix into a singly-bordered
L41@P1: block-diagonal (SB) form by utilizing the column-net hypergraph model [7–9]. The 2Dpartitioning-based method relies on transforming a sparse matrix into a doubly-bordered

L69@P2: The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Background material is introduced in Section 2. In Section 3, we review some of the previous works about iteration/data reordering

L72@P2: 2. Background. Several sparse-matrix storage schemes utilized in SpMxV are summarized in Section 2.1. Data locality issues during the SpMxV operation are discussed in

L75@P2: 2.1. Sparse-matrix storage schemes. There are two standard sparse-matrix storage
L76@P2: schemes for the SpMxV operation: Compressed Storage by Rows (CSR) and Compressed
L77@P2: Storage by Columns (CSC) [14, 33]. In this paper, we restrict our focus on the conventional
L78@P2: SpMxV operation using the CSR storage scheme without loss of generality, whereas cache
L79@P2: aware techniques such as prefetching, blocking, etc. are out of the scope of this paper. In the
L80@P2: following paragraphs, we review the standard CSR scheme and two CSR variants.

L86@P2: CSR storage scheme for an m×n sparse matrix. Each outer for-loop iteration of Algorithm 1
L87@P2: corresponds to the inner product of the respective sparse row with the dense input vector x.
